body:
Bhakti and the rise of Tamil saint-poets

Bhakti means loving devotion to a deity. In medieval India, several saint-poets taught that sincere devotion could bring a person closer to the divine. Many expressed their ideas through songs in languages understood by ordinary people rather than relying only on Sanskrit religious literature.

Among the earliest important regional traditions were those of the Alvars and Nayanars in Tamil-speaking South India. Their devotional traditions developed particularly between the 6th and 9th centuries CE. The two groups shared a commitment to personal devotion, but they worshipped different deities.

The essential distinction

Saint groupDeity and regionLanguagePrincipal collection
AlvarsVishnu; Tamil regionTamilNalayira Divya Prabandham
NayanarsShiva; Tamil regionTamilTevaram and Tiruvacakam

Both groups travelled to sacred places, sang hymns praising the deities worshipped there and helped establish lasting connections between Tamil devotional poetry and temple worship.

Alvars: devotees of Vishnu

The 12 Alvars were Vaishnava saint-poets. Important names include Nammalvar, Periyalvar, Andal and Tondaradippodi Alvar. Their compositions were collected in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, also called the Divya Prabandham. The collection came to be revered as the Tamil Veda.

Andal, a woman Alvar traditionally associated with Periyalvar as his daughter, is especially important. Her Tamil devotional compositions include the Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli. Her poetry expresses intense devotion to Vishnu. The presence of Andal shows that women were important contributors to early Tamil Bhakti literature.

Nayanars: devotees of Shiva

The 63 Nayanars belonged to the Shaiva devotional tradition. Four prominent names are Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar and Manikkavasagar.

The hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar form the principal body of the Tevaram. Manikkavasagar is particularly associated with the Tiruvacakam. These are Shaiva devotional works, not collections of Alvar hymns.

Remember the two pairings

Alvars: Vishnu, 12 saints, Divya Prabandham. Nayanars: Shiva, 63 saints, Tevaram and Tiruvacakam. Both traditions used Tamil.

From travelling songs to temple traditions

The Alvars and Nayanars came from varied social backgrounds, including groups considered low in the caste hierarchy. Their poetry gave importance to devotion and sometimes questioned the idea that birth alone determined religious worth. However, their teachings should not be treated as one uniform programme for abolishing every existing social distinction.

During the 10th to 12th centuries, Chola and Pandya rulers supported temples at many places associated with these saints. Their hymns were collected and incorporated into temple worship. Thus, poems originally sung by travelling devotees also became part of established religious institutions.

Prelims focus

  • 12 Alvars were devoted to Vishnu; 63 Nayanars were devoted to Shiva.
  • Both groups composed devotional poetry in Tamil.
  • Nalayira Divya Prabandham is the Alvar collection.
  • Tevaram is associated with Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar.
  • Tiruvacakam is associated with Manikkavasagar; Tiruppavai with Andal.
  • Trap: Do not interchange the Alvar and Nayanar texts merely because both originated in Tamil Nadu.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, 'Devotional Paths to the Divine', 2020–21 text, printed pp. 105–106; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Chapter 6, 'Bhakti-Sufi Traditions', printed pp. 143–146; University of Mumbai, Sambhashan, 'Andal: Afterlife of a 9th Century Woman Poet', p. 67.]

title: Tamil Bhakti Traditions: Alvars and Nayanars

body:
Vitthala devotion and the Marathi language

From the 13th century onwards, Maharashtra became an important centre of regional Bhakti. Its saint-poets expressed devotion in Marathi, making religious ideas accessible to people who did not study Sanskrit.

A central focus was Vitthala, also called Vithoba, worshipped at Pandharpur and regarded as a form of Vishnu or Krishna. The associated Varkari tradition placed importance on devotion, the remembrance of God's name, devotional singing and pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

Jnaneshwar: explaining spiritual ideas in Marathi

Jnaneshwar, also spelled Dnyaneshwar or Jnanadeva, was a major saint and religious thinker of 13th-century Maharashtra. His best-known work is the Jnaneshwari, also known as Bhavarthadipika.

The Jnaneshwari is a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita. It explains spiritual ideas through the regional language rather than simply reproducing the Sanskrit text. Another important work associated with Jnaneshwar is Amritanubhava.

Jnaneshwar is therefore remembered both as a Bhakti saint and as an important figure in the development of Marathi religious literature.

Namdev: devotional songs and a wider literary legacy

Namdev, also called Namadeva, was another major saint of Maharashtra, associated with the 13th–14th centuries. He was devoted to Vitthala and is especially remembered for devotional songs and hymns, including abhangs.

What is an abhang?

An abhang is a form of Marathi devotional verse or hymn strongly associated with Maharashtra's Bhakti tradition.

Namdev's influence was not limited to Maharashtra. Hymns attributed to him are also preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the sacred scripture of the Sikhs. This is an example of how devotional compositions travelled beyond their original regional setting.

The distinction is important: Namdev's hymns appear in the Guru Granth Sahib, but he was not the compiler of that scripture.

Comparison of the two saints

SaintRegionLanguagePrincipal literary association
JnaneshwarMaharashtraMarathiJnaneshwari; Amritanubhava
NamdevMaharashtraMarathi devotional traditionAbhangs and hymns; some preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib

Why Pandharpur matters

The Varkari tradition connects a deity, a place and a regional devotional practice: Vitthala is worshipped at Pandharpur, devotees travel there on pilgrimage, and Marathi devotional songs express their faith. The tradition demonstrates that Bhakti was not confined to reading a particular book; it also involved shared singing and religious gatherings.

Prelims focus

  • Jnaneshwar and Namdev are associated with Maharashtra.
  • Marathi is the principal language of their regional Bhakti tradition.
  • Jnaneshwari is Jnaneshwar's Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita.
  • Vitthala and Pandharpur are closely associated with the Varkari tradition.
  • Namdev is associated with abhangs; some of his hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Trap: Jnaneshwari is not a work of Namdev or Tulsidas.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, 'Devotional Paths to the Divine', 2020–21 text, printed pp. 108–109 and 118; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Chapter 6, 'Bhakti-Sufi Traditions', printed pp. 147 and 167; Vision IAS, Important Themes for Medieval History and Art and Culture, 2024, section 'Bhakti Literature in Regional Languages', pp. 21–23.]

pictures.alt: The Varkari tradition in Maharashtra connects Vitthala, worship at Pandharpur, Marathi abhangs, pilgrimage and devotional singing.
pictures.caption: The main elements of the Varkari tradition.

title: Maharashtra's Bhakti Saints: Jnaneshwar and Namdev

body:
Understanding nirguna devotion

In the study of Bhakti, an important distinction is made between nirguna and saguna devotion.

Nirguna means without qualities or form. In nirguna Bhakti, the Supreme Reality is understood as beyond a fixed physical image. Devotion, remembrance of the divine and personal spiritual experience are more important than worshipping a particular visible form.

Saguna means with qualities or form. A saguna devotee may worship God as Rama, Krishna, Shiva or another recognisable divine form.

Kabir and Ravidas are closely associated with the northern Indian Sant tradition, which emphasised devotion, inner spiritual experience and criticism of religious or social discrimination.

Kabir: devotion to the formless Supreme

Kabir is associated with Varanasi (Banaras) and the 15th–16th centuries. Accounts of his life are not completely reliable. A widely accepted tradition places his upbringing in a family of julahas, or weavers, in or near Varanasi.

Kabir rejected the idea that religious truth depended on caste, priestly authority or outward ritual. He criticised empty formalism among both Hindus and Muslims. His verses used names such as Ram and Allah for the divine, while emphasising one formless Supreme Reality.

His poetry circulated in forms of spoken Hindi and related northern Indian dialects, including the literary language often called Sant Bhasha. Important forms of his compositions include sakhis, short instructive verses, and pads, devotional lyrics. Kabir is also widely associated with dohas, or couplets.

Which text belongs to Kabir?

The most important association is the Bijak. However, it is more accurate to describe the Bijak as a later compilation of verses attributed to Kabir than as a complete book personally written and assembled by him.

Other collections preserving verses attributed to Kabir include the Kabir Granthavali and the Adi Granth, now contained within the Guru Granth Sahib. These different collections show how Kabir's teachings were preserved by several communities.

Kabir and Sikandar Lodi

Sikandar Lodi was Sultan of Delhi from 1489 to 1517. Later traditions and religious biographies describe Kabir facing persecution under Sikandar Lodi. This is an important association to recognise, but the particular persecution stories are traditional accounts, not securely established historical events. Kabir's life and exact chronology remain uncertain.

Ravidas: devotion and social equality

Ravidas, also called Raidas, is associated with the Varanasi region of present-day Uttar Pradesh. His verses belong to the northern Indian vernacular devotional tradition and are commonly associated with Hindi and related dialects.

Ravidas stressed that sincere devotion and human worth were not determined by caste or inherited social status. Traditions describe him as belonging to a community of leather workers. His teachings challenged the idea that occupation or birth made a person spiritually inferior.

Hymns attributed to Ravidas are included in the Guru Granth Sahib. This is a crucial text association. The scripture contains compositions from several devotional traditions; inclusion does not make every contributing saint a Sikh Guru.

Some traditions also identify Ravidas as Mirabai's spiritual teacher. This association is useful for identifying the connection between two Bhakti figures, but the historical relationship cannot be established with certainty from the surviving accounts.

Kabir and Ravidas compared

SaintRegion and languageMajor textual associationCentral emphasis
KabirVaranasi; Hindi-related vernaculars and Sant BhashaBijak; Kabir Granthavali; hymns in Guru Granth SahibFormless Supreme; criticism of ritualism and caste
RavidasVaranasi region; Hindi-related vernacularsHymns in Guru Granth SahibDevotion, equality and rejection of caste-based spiritual superiority

Prelims focus

  • Kabir and Ravidas are associated with the Varanasi region.
  • Kabir is a major figure of nirguna Bhakti.
  • Bijak is associated with Kabir's verses.
  • Verses of both Kabir and Ravidas are preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Sikandar Lodi ruled from 1489 to 1517; stories connecting his persecution of Kabir are traditional.
  • Trap: The Guru Granth Sahib preserves the hymns of several saints; it was not composed in its entirety by Kabir, Ravidas or Namdev.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, 'Devotional Paths to the Divine', 2020–21 text, printed pp. 114–117; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Chapter 6, 'Bhakti-Sufi Traditions', printed pp. 161–165; Prabhakar Machwe, Kabir, Sahitya Akademi, 'Life', p. 14; UNESCO, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Volume IV, Part 1, section 'The Lodis', p. 295.]

pictures.caption: Artisans and listeners in the world of North Indian vernacular Bhakti.

title: Kabir and Ravidas: Nirguna Bhakti in North India

body:
Saguna Bhakti through familiar divine forms

Saguna Bhakti centres on devotion to God understood through recognisable qualities and forms. In medieval North India, Rama and Krishna, both regarded as forms of Vishnu, became important centres of devotional poetry.

Tulsidas is particularly associated with Rama, while Surdas and Mirabai are particularly associated with Krishna. Their works also show the importance of distinguishing Awadhi, Braj Bhasha and Rajasthani.

Tulsidas: Rama devotion in Awadhi

Tulsidas was a major saint-poet associated with Uttar Pradesh, especially the Awadh and Varanasi regions, in the 16th–17th centuries. His most famous work is the Ramcharitmanas, composed in Awadhi.

The Ramcharitmanas retells the story of Rama as a devotional work in a regional language. Its importance lies partly in making the Rama narrative accessible to a much wider audience.

Tulsidas – Rama – Awadhi – Ramcharitmanas. This is a complete four-part matching relationship.

Surdas: Krishna devotion in Braj Bhasha

Surdas is associated with the Braj region of western Uttar Pradesh. His devotional poetry celebrates Krishna, including the affection, love and emotional attachment felt by Krishna's devotees.

The principal language associated with Surdas is Braj Bhasha, an important literary form of Hindi.

Three major works traditionally associated with Surdas are Sursagar, Surasaravali and Sahitya Lahari. The Sursagar is especially well known as a collection of Krishna-devotional poetry. As with many medieval poetic collections, the complete surviving body of verses should not automatically be assumed to have been personally composed or arranged by Surdas in its present form.

Surdas – Krishna – Braj Bhasha – Sursagar. The names Surasaravali and Sahitya Lahari are additional important associations.

Mirabai: Krishna devotion across Rajasthan and Gujarat

Mirabai was a woman saint-poet associated with Merta in Marwar and the royal family of Mewar, both in present-day Rajasthan. She is remembered for intense personal devotion to Krishna.

Her devotional songs are commonly called bhajans or pads. The poetry attributed to her survives in Rajasthani and Braj-related forms, along with versions transmitted in other regional languages.

Unlike Tulsidas, who is firmly identified with a major extended composition, Mirabai is best identified with a body of devotional songs. They were passed down orally for generations. Consequently, it is difficult to determine which surviving verses were composed by Mirabai herself and which acquired her name during later transmission.

Her songs express Krishna devotion in deeply personal terms and often challenge the expectations placed on a woman from a royal household. Some traditions identify Ravidas as her teacher, although that relationship is not historically certain.

Mirabai's Gujarat connection

Mirabai's songs became especially popular in Rajasthan and Gujarat. Gujarati versions and local devotional traditions helped preserve and circulate poetry attributed to her. This is a genuine connection with Gujarat's cultural history, but Mirabai should not be classified simply as a Gujarati-language poet: her main historical association is with Rajasthan and the Rajasthani-Braj devotional world.

Three different literary situations

These saints are best distinguished not only by deity and language but also by the way their compositions have survived.

  • Tulsidas: A major identifiable literary composition, the Ramcharitmanas, in Awadhi.
  • Surdas: Krishna-devotional verses preserved in collections such as Sursagar, written in the Braj literary tradition.
  • Mirabai: Devotional songs transmitted widely through oral and regional singing traditions, without one securely established original collected book.

Prelims focus

  • Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi; his devotion centred on Rama.
  • Surdas is associated with Braj Bhasha, Krishna and Sursagar.
  • Surasaravali and Sahitya Lahari are also traditionally associated with Surdas.
  • Mirabai was associated with Merta and Mewar in Rajasthan and was devoted to Krishna.
  • Mirabai's songs became popular in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
  • Trap: Ramcharitmanas is an Awadhi work; Sursagar belongs to the Braj devotional tradition.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 8, 'Devotional Paths to the Divine', 2020–21 text, printed pp. 113–115; NCERT, Themes in Indian History – Part II, Class 12, Chapter 6, 'Bhakti-Sufi Traditions', printed pp. 164–165; CBSE, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Module 3.2, 'Indian Literatures – Part 2', section 'Mirabai: Bhajans', p. 52.]

pictures.alt: Tulsidas is linked to an identifiable composition, Surdas to poetry collections, and Mirabai to orally transmitted songs with uncertain individual attribution.
pictures.caption: Three ways medieval devotional literature has been preserved.

title: Tulsidas, Surdas and Mirabai: Devotion to Rama and Krishna
